evidence_after.text: This is mostly due to the availability of language resources for English. To address this shortcoming, this paper presents the ﬁrst Greek annotated dataset for offensive language identiﬁcation: the Offensive Greek Tweet Dataset (OGTD). OGTD is a manually annotated dataset containing 4,779 posts from Twitter annotated as offensive and not offensive. Along with a detailed description of the dataset, we evaluate several computational models trained and tested on this data.

evidence_after.title: Offensive Language Identification in Greek
evidence_after.text: The complete results are presented in table 5 below. The experiment with linguistic features was the combina- tion of dependency relation tags with TF/IDF unigrams. This experimented yielded the same F1-score of 80% as the other Linear SVM classiﬁers, performing almost iden- tically with the previous model trained with POS tags, only bested in precision for the Offensive class.

evidence_after.title: Offensive Language Identification in Greek
evidence_after.text: In the next experiment, POS tags were used in conjunction with TF/IDF unigram features. Surprisingly, the addition of POS tags in the Linear SVM yields the same F1-score as the ﬁrst model trained on TF/IDF unigram features, yield- ing lower precision scores for both classes, while the re- call score for the Offensive class improved marginally. The Naïve Bayes models show a marginal decrease in their per- formance.

evidence_after.title: Offensive Language Identification in Greek
evidence_after.text: Offensive Language Identiﬁcation in Greek Zeses Pitenis1, Marcos Zampieri2, Tharindu Ranasinghe1 1University of Wolverhampton - Wolverhampton, UK 2Rochester Institute of Technology - Rochester, NY, USA z.pitenis@wlv.ac.uk, marcos.zampieri@rit.edu, tharindu.ranasinghe@wlv.ac.uk As offensive language has become a rising issue for online communities and social media platforms, researchers have been investigating ways of coping with abusive content and developing systems to detect its different types: cyberbullying, hate speech, aggression, etc. With a few notable exceptions, most research on this topic so far has dealt with English.

evidence_after.text: 4.3. Discussion The data annotated in OGTD proved to be facilitating in offensive language detection with a signiﬁcant success for Greek, taking into consideration its size and label distri- bution, with the best model (LSTM and GRU with Atten- tion) achieving a F1-macro of 0.89. Among the classi- cal machine learning approaches, the linear SVM model achieved the best results, 0.80, whereas the the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) learning classiﬁer yielded the best recall score for the Offensive class, at 0.61. In terms of features used, TF/IDF matrices of word unigrams proved to work work well with multiple classical ML classiﬁers.
